picks.title: Brain scans may explain why deepfake faces appear 'hyperreal'
picks.rationale: fMRI study (126 people aged 18-89, Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience): people rated AI-generated faces as more real than real photos, and anterior-insula activity dropped for deepfakes. Older adults showed the strongest bias, which gives a neural basis for 'AI hyperrealism'.
picks.excerpt: University of Florida psychologist Natalie Ebner's team showed 126 people aged 18-89 a set of 80 real and AI-generated faces while scanning their brains. Participants rated the deepfakes as more real than the real photos, and activity in the anterior insula dropped when they viewed deepfakes. Older adults showed the strongest bias (Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience).

picks.title: Chat-based AI lets users run complex alloy calculations on their own computers
picks.rationale: Empa's OptiMat Alloys (npj Computational Materials) is a knowledge-grounded agent framework that lets materials scientists run atomistic high-entropy-alloy simulations by plain-text chat, computed locally on their own machine. It changes the method for computational materials work.
picks.excerpt: Empa researchers (Yang Hu et al.) built OptiMat Alloys, an AI agent framework that lets materials scientists run atomistic high-entropy-alloy simulations through a plain text chat. It is grounded in scientific knowledge and computes results on demand on the user's own computer (npj Computational Materials).

picks.title: Using Vibrations and AI, Future Robotic Missions Could Handle Buried Rocks Autonomously
picks.rationale: Virginia Tech (IEEE Sensors Journal) uses AI on surface vibrations to estimate how deep partly buried rocks go, so energy-limited lunar and Mars robots can decide on their own whether to dig out an obstacle or steer around it. It adds a planetary-exploration lane to the deck.
picks.excerpt: Virginia Tech's Yiyan Ruan and Erik Komendera (a former NASA Langley researcher) use AI to read surface vibrations and estimate how deep partly buried rocks go. This would let energy-limited robots on the Moon or Mars decide on their own whether to dig out an obstacle or steer around it (IEEE Sensors Journal).

picks.title: Dark matter-hunting satellite Euclid reveals record number of cosmic 'magnifying glasses'
picks.rationale: Euclid's first data release (DR1) yields about 15,000 strong-lens candidates, against fewer than 1,000 confirmed before. Machine learning does the first-pass sort of the survey and citizen scientists refine the AI-ranked pool, and the team aims for an ML model that confirms lenses without human checks. This is a real ML-plus-crowd discovery pipeline at survey scale, but AI is one stage of it, so the copy must not overclaim.
picks.excerpt: Euclid's first major data release (DR1) yields about 15,000 new strong-gravitational-lens candidates; before Euclid there were fewer than 1,000 confirmed lenses. In the UBC-involved four-step search, machine learning first sorts the huge dataset for likely lenses, then thousands of citizen scientists refine the AI-sorted pool, and the team aims to build an ML model that can confirm lenses without human checks. Note: AI is one stage of the pipeline, not the headline.
